mainText:
If you only remember one thing today: Meta just joined the top tier of A I, and at the same time Wall Street is asking whether anyone can afford the build-out.

Number one. The A I frontier gets crowded.

Meta released its new Muse Wonder models, code-named Watermelon. From your Rundown newsletter: the bigger version now ranks second overall on Artificial Analysis, behind only Anthropic's Opus five point five. Google's Gemini four Argon, open g p t six Astra, and Claude Fable five point one are all bunched just below. Unlike Meta's old open Llama models, these are closed, and Meta says its prices will undercut Open A I and Anthropic.

Google also opened Gemini four Argon to Pro and Ultra subscribers this week. It handles up to one million tokens and targets long, multi-step work like finance, legal, and coding. Your A I Collective newsletter notes the A P I price doubles on December first.

Why it matters: the frontier used to be a two-horse race. Now it's three, and Meta brings billions of users with it.

Number two. The A I money question.

From your Politico Decoded newsletter: bank chiefs on earnings calls are getting cautious. Jamie Dimon cited short-term vulnerabilities from rising interest rates. Goldman's David Solomon said nobody knows if borrowing costs could become a chokepoint. One estimate puts the A I build-out at over ten trillion dollars through twenty thirty two. Tech stocks fell last week on news that Open A I's revenue was lower than assumed. And Anthropic is reportedly updating investors today, ahead of a possible I P O as soon as next month.

Why it matters: the technology may be solid, but the financing is what could shake markets.

Number three. A I and security.

Federal prosecutors charged an Open A I engineer with hiding a recording device in an executive meeting room in San Francisco. Open A I says its own models helped trace the device to him. A U S attorney called it a matter of national security.

Separately, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moved his forecast for A I fully improving itself to twenty twenty seven, one year earlier than before.

Why it matters: A I labs now guard their conversations like state secrets, and the race to automate A I research is speeding up.

Number four. Policy and Europe.

In Dublin today, the E U-backed International A I Summit is underway. Politico reports Europe is quietly stepping back from the frontier race. Even France's Mistral faces questions. The new line is that Europe doesn't need to own the models. Also, a Wisconsin governor candidate is running on an A I safety platform, a sign A I is entering midterm politics.

Why it matters: Europe is shifting from building A I to regulating and using it.

Number five. Social media and the media industry.

Facebook now lets you type, in your own words, what you want to see in your feed and Reels. And a Pentagon plan to livestream an execution is putting social platforms in a bind, since their rules bar graphic death, but enforcing them could cause political backlash.

For comms folks, your Comms Stack newsletter flags that journalists are getting A I reputation scores, and a federal judge ruled that nobody owes publishers traffic from Google's A I Overviews.

Why it matters: platforms and courts are redefining who controls what audiences see.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker covers the doxing of a Cornell student. Noosphere reports migrant children facing deportation are losing funding for lawyers. And Recode China A I asks whether we really understand Chinese A I voices, after a DeepSeek researcher's blog sparked controversy.

Good news to close. Karpathy reminds us that nearly six billion people have barely used A I. That's a huge opening for tools that serve them, and for people who explain A I well.

The thread today: A I is getting more powerful and more expensive at the same time. Have a great day, Sin.
